tool.name: Keras
tool.tagline: High-level deep learning API that runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch
tool.description: Keras is a high-level API for building and training neural networks with layers, models, fit() and callbacks. Keras 3 is multi-backend: the same model code runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, chosen with one setting. It is the fastest way to go from idea to trained model, and it scales to custom training steps and distributed training when you need them.

glossary.def: One of the adjustable numbers inside a model. Training changes the weights; everything the model has learned is stored in them.
An extra learned number a layer adds to each output, like b in w * x + b, so the output need not be zero when the input is.
Short for loss function: the single number that says how wrong a model's guesses are on some examples. Training tries to push it down.
One building block of a neural network: it takes numbers in, does one kind of arithmetic with its own weights, and passes numbers on to the next layer.
The most common layer: every output is a weighted sum of every input plus a bias, usually followed by an activation function.
A simple non-linear function applied to each number a layer outputs, such as ReLU (replace negatives with 0). Without it, stacked layers could only learn straight-line relationships.
A function that turns a list of raw scores into probabilities: all positive and adding up to 1, with the biggest score getting the biggest share.
The raw scores a model outputs before softmax turns them into probabilities. Higher means 'more likely', but they are not yet between 0 and 1.
The method that turns gradients into weight updates: plain gradient descent, or smarter variants such as Adam that adapt the step size for each weight.

A score that tells you how well a model is doing, such as accuracy, reported during training and evaluation; unlike the loss it is only for you to read. (Elsewhere, any number measured about a system.)
The share of predictions that were right, e.g. 0.95 means 95 out of 100 correct. The most common metric for classification.
In Keras 3, the library that actually stores tensors and does the arithmetic: JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch. Keras code stays the same whichever you pick. (Elsewhere, the server side of an app.)
Google's custom chip built only for the matrix arithmetic of neural networks, rented through Google Cloud; often faster than GPUs for large models.
A layer that slides a small window of learned weights (say 3x3 pixels) across an image and computes a weighted sum at each position, so it can spot the same pattern anywhere.
In a convolution or pooling layer, how many pixels the window moves each step; a stride of 2 halves the height and width.
Adding a border of zeros around an image (or dummy values to short sequences) so sizes line up; 'same' padding keeps a convolution's output the size of its input.
Shrinking an image-like tensor by summarising each small block (or the whole image) with its maximum or average value.
In Keras, a layer's main table of weights, e.g. the (inputs, units) matrix of a Dense layer or the windows of a convolution. (Elsewhere, the kernel is an operating system's core program.)
Keras's way of building a model by calling layers on placeholder inputs and wrapping the result in keras.Model(inputs, outputs); it allows branches, merges and several inputs or outputs.
Adding a block's input back onto its output (x + f(x)), which lets very deep networks train well; ResNet models are built from them.
Running inputs through the model to get its outputs. The gradients are then worked out by going backwards over the same steps.
Predicting which of a fixed set of categories (classes) an input belongs to, such as spam or not spam, or which digit a picture shows.
Predicting a number, such as a price or a temperature, rather than a category.
The standard loss for classification: small when the model gives the right class a high probability, large when it is confidently wrong.
Writing a category as a list of zeros with a single 1 at that category's position, e.g. class 2 of 4 is [0, 0, 1, 0].
Regression losses: the average of the squared (or, for mean absolute error, the plain) differences between predictions and right answers.
A rule that changes the learning rate as training goes on, e.g. starting small (warm-up), then shrinking it smoothly so late steps make finer adjustments.
Shrinking every weight a tiny bit at each step, which keeps weights small and makes memorising the training data harder.
Capping how large gradients may get before the update, so one unusual batch can't throw the weights far off.
Ending training automatically when the score on validation data stops improving, usually keeping the best weights seen.
Any technique that makes a model generalise better instead of memorising, such as dropout, weight penalties or data augmentation.
A layer that, during training only, randomly sets a fraction of its inputs to zero, so the model can't depend on any single number and overfits less.
A layer that rescales the numbers flowing through it to a steady average and spread, which makes training faster and more stable; it keeps running averages for use after training.
Making extra training examples by randomly altering real ones, e.g. flipping, rotating or zooming images, so the model sees more variety.
Turning raw data into the form a model wants: scaling numbers to a small range, mapping categories or words to integer ids, resizing images.
A value a lookup layer never saw when it learned its list of known values; it is mapped to a reserved index instead of failing.
TensorFlow's module for loading and preparing data step by step and handing it to the model in batches.
PyTorch's object for loading a dataset in shuffled batches, optionally with several worker processes.
TensorFlow's folder format for a finished model that other TensorFlow tools (servers, phone runtimes) can load without your Python code.
Open Neural Network Exchange: a shared file format for trained models that many tools and devices can run, whichever library trained them.
In Keras on JAX, code that keeps no hidden changing values: the current weights go in as arguments and the new weights come out as results.
Starting from a model already trained on a big dataset and reusing what it learned for your own, usually smaller, task.
A big public collection of over a million labelled photos in 1,000 categories, the standard dataset for training image models that others then reuse.
The official Keras library of ready-to-use pretrained models for text, images and audio, including large language models.
A generative adversarial network: two models trained against each other, one making fake examples and one trying to tell fakes from real ones.
Doing most arithmetic with 16-bit floats (half the usual size, much faster on modern GPUs) while keeping the weights themselves in 32-bit so small updates aren't lost.
A Keras setting that says which dtype each layer computes in and which it stores its weights in, e.g. compute in bfloat16, store in float32.
A 16-bit floating-point number: about 3 decimal digits of precision and a small range (largest value 65504). Fast on GPUs but easy to underflow.
A 16-bit float with the same range as float32 but fewer digits of precision; used on TPUs and newer GPUs because it rarely underflows.
When a number is too small for its type to represent and becomes 0; in float16 anything below about 0.00000006 vanishes.
Multiplying the loss by a large number before computing gradients so tiny gradients don't underflow in float16, then dividing them back before the update.
Special units in newer NVIDIA GPUs that multiply small 16-bit matrices extremely fast; the reason mixed precision gives big speedups.
A popular library for building neural networks on top of JAX.
Splitting one big tensor, such as a weight matrix or a batch, into pieces held by different devices, so together they can handle more than one device could.
A grid that arranges the available GPUs or TPU cores along named axes (e.g. 'batch' and 'model'), used to say how tensors are split across them.
Training with a full copy of the model on every device and a different slice of each batch on each, then combining their gradients.
Splitting a model's weights across several devices because it is too big for one, with each device computing its part.
Python's compiled, low-level form of a function. Loading it from a file can run whatever code its author wrote, which is why Keras refuses it by default.

concepts.name: Models, training and Keras
concepts.summary: Keras builds and trains neural networks: models whose numbers are learned from examples. This lesson explains model, weights, loss and gradient in plain words.
concepts.why: Every Keras function talks about models, layers, training, losses and gradients; this lesson gives you those words before you need them.
concepts.body:
Suppose you want a program that reads a photo and says which digit, 0 to 9, it shows. Writing the rules by hand is hopeless. **Machine learning** takes the other route: you collect many examples with the right answers attached (the **training data**) and let the computer find the pattern itself.

What it finds is a **model**: a fixed formula with many adjustable numbers inside. Those numbers are the model's **weights**. Feed in an input (the pixels), the model does arithmetic with its weights, and out comes a guess. With random weights the guesses are nonsense; with good weights they are right.

**Training** is the search for good weights. It repeats one loop:

- Run a few examples through the model and look at its guesses.
- Score how wrong they are with a **loss function**: one number that is zero for perfect guesses and grows the worse they get.
- Work out, for every weight, which way to nudge it to make the loss smaller. That set of directions is the **gradient**.
- Nudge every weight a small step that way, and repeat until the loss stops falling.

The kind of model Keras builds is a **neural network**: a stack of **layers**. Each layer takes numbers from the one before, combines them using its own weights, and passes new numbers on. Many simple layers stacked together can recognise digits, faces or spoken words.

Inside, the numbers travel as **tensors**: grids of numbers with any number of dimensions, like NumPy arrays. A **batch** (a group of examples processed together) of 32 small greyscale images is a tensor of shape `(32, 28, 28)`.

Keras gives you the layers ready-made, works out gradients for you, and runs the whole loop with one call, `fit()`. It runs fast on a **GPU** (a graphics chip that does thousands of multiplications at once) when you have one. You do not need the maths to start, only these words: model, weights, layer, loss, gradient, training.
concepts.code:
# A toy "model" with one weight w: guess = w * x.   The truth is y = 3 * x.
w = 0.0
examples = [(1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9)]            # (input, correct answer)

def loss(w):                                    # 0 when every guess is perfect
    return sum((w * x - y) ** 2 for x, y in examples)

for step in range(20):
    # gradient: how much the loss rises if w grows a tiny bit
    grad = (loss(w + 0.001) - loss(w)) / 0.001
    w -= 0.01 * grad                            # step the other way, lowering the loss

print(round(w, 2), round(loss(w), 4))           # 3.0 0.0003  -> it learned y = 3x
# Keras does the same for millions of weights, computing gradients exactly.
takeaways: A model is a formula with adjustable weights; training finds good values for them
The loss measures how wrong the model is; the gradient says which way to nudge each weight
A neural network is a stack of layers; Keras provides them and runs training with fit()
pitfalls: Judging a model only by how well it does on its own training data: a low loss there can mean it memorised the examples rather than learned the pattern.

quiz.q: What changes while a model trains?
quiz.explain: Training keeps the data and the model's structure fixed and adjusts its weights to lower the loss.

quiz.q: What does a loss function return?
options: One number saying how wrong the model's guesses are
quiz.explain: The loss is a single score; training tries to make it as small as possible.

concepts.name: Keras 3 and its backends
concepts.summary: Keras 3 runs the same model code on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch; choose which one with KERAS_BACKEND before importing keras.
concepts.why: Choosing a backend is the first decision in a Keras 3 project; it affects speed, how you can ship the model and which other code you can mix in.
concepts.body:
Keras doesn't do the number-crunching itself. It hands that work to a **backend**: a separate library that stores the tensors, computes gradients and talks to the GPU. Keras 3 supports three: `"jax"` (JAX, from Google), `"tensorflow"` (TensorFlow, also Google) and `"torch"` (PyTorch, from Meta). You write models, layers and losses once against Keras, and the backend runs them.

Choose the backend before Keras is imported, with the `KERAS_BACKEND` **environment variable** (a named setting a program reads when it starts; `os.environ` sets one from Python) or the `"backend"` field of `~/.keras/keras.json`. Once Keras is imported, the backend stays fixed until the program restarts. `keras.config.backend()` tells you which one is active.

Why the choice matters:

- JAX is often the fastest for training, because it compiles the whole calculation into optimised code, and it runs well on Google's **TPU** chips.
- TensorFlow has the most tools for shipping a finished model into apps and onto phones.
- PyTorch lets Keras models mix with PyTorch code: a Keras model is also a `torch.nn.Module`.

Tensors you get back belong to the backend (a `jax.Array`, `tf.Tensor` or `torch.Tensor`), but every Keras function also accepts NumPy arrays. Install with `pip install keras` plus the backend library you want. Two extra backends, `"numpy"` and `"openvino"`, can only run finished models, not train them.

In TensorFlow 2.16 and later, `tf.keras` is also Keras 3. Old Keras 2 code that relies on TensorFlow internals may need updates; the `tf_keras` package keeps Keras 2 available.
concepts.code:
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"      # or "tensorflow" / "torch"; set BEFORE import

import keras

print(keras.__version__)                 # 3.x
print(keras.config.backend())            # jax

x = keras.ops.convert_to_tensor([1.0, 2.0])
print(type(x).__module__)                # a native jax array type under JAX
print(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras.ops.sum(x * 2)))   # 6.0
takeaways: One codebase, three backends: JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch
Set `KERAS_BACKEND` before importing keras
Returned tensors belong to the backend; NumPy inputs work everywhere
pitfalls: Setting `KERAS_BACKEND` after `import keras`, which has no effect.

quiz.q: You set os.environ['KERAS_BACKEND'] = 'torch' after import keras ran. Which backend is used?
options: The backend chosen at import time
quiz.explain: The backend is fixed when Keras is first imported; later changes to the variable are ignored.

concepts.name: The Sequential model
concepts.summary: Stack layers in keras.Sequential, declare the shape of one example with keras.Input, and inspect the model with summary().
concepts.why: Sequential is the quickest way to define the many models that are a plain stack of layers.
concepts.body:
`keras.Sequential` builds a model from a list of layers, each passing its output to the next. Start the list with `keras.Input(shape=...)`, which declares the shape of **one example**, say 784 numbers for a flattened 28x28 image, so the model can create its weights right away.

Models always work on a **batch**: a group of examples processed together. Every tensor flowing through the model therefore has an extra first dimension for the batch. It shows as `None` in shapes because any **batch size** (number of examples per batch) works, and you never include it in `keras.Input`.

Once built you can:

- `model.summary()` to print each layer's output shape and parameter count ("parameters" is Keras's word for the weights).
- `model.count_params()`, `model.layers`, `model.weights`, `model.output_shape`.
- Call `model(x)` on a batch to get predictions, returned as backend tensors.

A `Dense(units)` layer has `inputs * units + units` parameters: one weight per input-output pair, plus one **bias** per output (a learned number it adds on, like `b` in `w * x + b`).

Without an `Input`, the model creates its weights the first time it sees data, and `summary()` is unavailable until then.

Sequential fits when there is exactly one input, one output and nothing branching. For models with several inputs or outputs, use the functional API (a later lesson); for arbitrary Python logic, subclass `keras.Model`. You can also `model.add(layer)` and `model.pop()` to edit a Sequential model step by step.
concepts.code:
import keras
from keras import layers

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(784,)),            # one sample = 784 features
    layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dropout(0.2),                  # randomly zeroes 20% while training
    layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),   # 10 class probabilities
], name="mnist_mlp")

model.summary()                           # layers, output shapes, parameter counts
print(model.count_params())               # 101770  (784*128+128 + 128*10+10)
print(model.output_shape)                 # (None, 10)
print(len(model.layers))                  # 3
print(tuple(model.layers[0].kernel.shape))   # (784, 128)
takeaways: Start with `keras.Input(shape=...)`: the shape of one example
`summary()` shows output shapes and parameter counts
Sequential = one input, one output, no branches
pitfalls: Including the batch size in `keras.Input(shape=...)`.

quiz.q: For images of 28x28 pixels with 1 channel, what should keras.Input receive?
quiz.explain: Input takes the shape of one example (height, width, colour channels last); Keras adds the batch dimension itself.

concepts.name: Core layers
concepts.summary: The layers you will use most, from Dense to Conv2D and Embedding: what each one does and how it changes the shape of the data.
concepts.why: Models are assembled from these layers; knowing their shapes lets you design models and track down mistakes in them.
concepts.body:
Keras layers are objects you call like functions: they hold weights and transform tensors. The one you have already met is **`Dense(units, activation=...)`**: each output is a weighted sum of all the inputs plus a bias. It works on the last axis, so `(batch, 20)` becomes `(batch, units)`.

The `activation` is an **activation function** applied to every output. `"relu"` turns negative numbers into 0; `"gelu"` is a smooth cousin of it; `"softmax"` turns a row of scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Without one, stacked layers could only learn straight-line relationships. Activations can also be separate `Activation` layers.

For images, `Conv2D(filters, kernel_size)` performs a **convolution**: it slides a small window, say 3x3 pixels, across the image and computes a weighted sum at every position. Each of the `filters` windows has its own weights and learns to spot one pattern, such as an edge. Keras stores images **channels-last**: `(batch, height, width, channels)`, where channels are the colour values.

Two settings control the output size. With a **stride** of 2 (`strides=2`) the window jumps 2 pixels at a time, halving height and width. **Padding** adds a border of zeros: `padding="same"` keeps height and width unchanged at stride 1, while `"valid"` (the default) adds none, so a 3x3 window trims one pixel from each edge.

**Pooling** shrinks an image: `MaxPooling2D(2)` keeps the largest value in each 2x2 block, and `GlobalAveragePooling2D()` averages each channel over the whole image, leaving `(batch, channels)`. `Flatten()` turns everything after the batch axis into one long row.

`Embedding(input_dim, output_dim)` turns integer ids, such as word numbers, into rows of `output_dim` learned numbers, one row per id. That row is the id's **embedding**.

Layers for sequences (`LSTM`, `GRU`, `MultiHeadAttention`), normalisation layers and `Dropout` follow the same call-on-a-tensor pattern; later lessons use them.

A layer creates its weights the first time it sees an input (its `build` step), so `Conv2D(16, 3)` needn't know the number of input channels. Afterwards `layer.weights`, `layer.kernel` (the main weight table) and `layer.bias` exist. Calling a layer on a NumPy array is a quick way to check output shapes.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers

x = np.random.rand(2, 28, 28, 1).astype("float32")    # batch, height, width, channels
conv = layers.Conv2D(16, kernel_size=3, padding="same", activation="relu")
y = conv(x)
print(tuple(y.shape))                                   # (2, 28, 28, 16)
print(tuple(layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(y).shape))           # (2, 14, 14, 16)
print(tuple(conv.kernel.shape), tuple(conv.bias.shape)) # (3, 3, 1, 16) (16,)
print(tuple(layers.Flatten()(y).shape))                 # (2, 12544)
print(tuple(layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(y).shape))  # (2, 16)

emb = layers.Embedding(input_dim=1000, output_dim=8)
print(tuple(emb(np.array([[4, 20, 7]])).shape))         # (1, 3, 8)
takeaways: Keras images are channels-last: (batch, height, width, channels)
Layers create their weights on the first call
`padding='same'` keeps height and width at stride 1
pitfalls: Feeding images stored channels-first, as some other libraries do, without transposing them.

quiz.q: What is the output shape of Conv2D(32, 3) (default padding) on input (8, 64, 64, 3)?
quiz.explain: The default padding is 'valid', so a 3x3 window trims one pixel on each side: 64 -> 62.

concepts.name: compile, fit, evaluate, predict
concepts.summary: Set up training with compile(optimizer, loss, metrics), train with fit(), measure with evaluate() and get predictions with predict().
concepts.why: This four-call workflow trains the majority of Keras models in practice.
concepts.body:
Before training, **compile** the model with two essential choices:

- an **optimizer**, the method that turns gradients into weight updates: a name like `"adam"` (a popular, forgiving choice) or an object such as `keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3)` to set its options;
- a **loss**: the number training should push down.

You can also ask for **metrics**: extra scores, such as **accuracy** (the share of correct answers), that are reported as training goes. Unlike the loss, they are only for you to read.

**`fit(x, y, batch_size, epochs, validation_split, callbacks)`** runs the training loop. One **epoch** is one full pass through the training data; `epochs=20` repeats it 20 times. `fit` returns a `History` object whose `.history` dict holds the loss and metrics of every epoch.

`validation_split=0.2` holds back 20% of the examples as a **validation set**: data the model never trains on, used to check how it does on examples it hasn't seen. Its results appear with a `val_` prefix. It takes the **last** 20% without shuffling, so shuffle ordered data first.

**`evaluate(x, y)`** returns the loss and metrics on new data. **`predict(x)`** runs the model in batches and returns NumPy arrays.

Choose the loss and the last layer together. For **classification** (picking one of several classes) with integer labels, use `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy`, the standard **cross-entropy** loss.

If the last layer outputs raw scores (**logits**) with no softmax, pass `from_logits=True`, which is more numerically stable. For **regression** (predicting a number) use `"mse"` or `"mae"`, the average squared or absolute error.

`verbose=0` silences the progress bar, which is handy in scripts.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.random((1000, 8)).astype("float32")
y = (x[:, 0] + x[:, 1] > 1).astype("int32")

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((8,)),
                          layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
                          layers.Dense(2)])                  # raw scores (logits)
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
              loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
              metrics=["accuracy"])

history = model.fit(x, y, batch_size=32, epochs=20, validation_split=0.2, verbose=0)
print(list(history.history))   # includes 'loss', 'accuracy', 'val_loss', 'val_accuracy'

loss, acc = model.evaluate(x, y, verbose=0)
logits = model.predict(x[:2], verbose=0)
print(type(logits).__name__, logits.shape)                    # ndarray (2, 2)
takeaways: compile = optimizer + loss + metrics
fit returns History; evaluate measures; predict returns NumPy
`from_logits=True` when the last layer has no softmax
pitfalls: Using `validation_split` on sorted data, so the validation set contains only the last classes.

quiz.q: The final layer is Dense(10) with no activation and labels are integers 0-9. Which loss fits?
quiz.explain: Integer labels need the sparse version, and raw scores need from_logits=True.

concepts.name: The functional API
concepts.summary: Build models as networks of layers with several inputs or outputs, skip connections and shared layers, using keras.Model(inputs, outputs).
concepts.why: Most real models branch or merge; the functional API expresses them while keeping summary(), plotting and saving.
concepts.body:
In the **functional API** you build a model like a flowchart. `keras.Input` creates a placeholder for the input; calling a layer on a placeholder returns a new placeholder (a `KerasTensor`) that remembers which layer produced it; finally `keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=...)` turns the whole chain into a model. Every placeholder has a known shape, so shape mistakes show up while you build the model, not once training starts.

It handles what Sequential cannot:

- **Multiple inputs**, such as text plus a few numeric fields, merged with `layers.concatenate` or `layers.add`.
- **Multiple outputs**, each with its own loss (and optional `loss_weights`), passed to `compile` as a dict keyed by output layer names.
- **Skip connections**: adding a block's input back onto its output (`x = layers.add([x, shortcut])`), which helps very deep networks train; ResNet image models are built this way.
- **Shared layers**: calling the same layer object on two inputs reuses its weights, for example to compare two photos with one network.

The model is a fixed network of layers, so Keras can print it with `summary()`, draw it with `keras.utils.plot_model`, save and rebuild it completely, and give you any intermediate result with `keras.Model(model.input, model.get_layer("name").output)`.

When feeding data, pass dicts keyed by input names (`{"text": ..., "meta": ...}`) for clarity. A functional model is itself a layer, so you can call one model inside another.
concepts.code:
import keras
from keras import layers

text_in = keras.Input(shape=(100,), dtype="int32", name="text")   # 100 word ids per example
meta_in = keras.Input(shape=(5,), name="meta")

t = layers.Embedding(10_000, 32)(text_in)
t = layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D()(t)
m = layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")(meta_in)
h = layers.concatenate([t, m])

priority = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="priority")(h)  # 0-1 probability
dept = layers.Dense(4, name="dept")(h)                           # raw scores (logits)

model = keras.Model(inputs=[text_in, meta_in], outputs=[priority, dept])
model.compile(optimizer="adam",
              loss={"priority": "binary_crossentropy",
                    "dept": keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)})
print([tuple(o.shape) for o in model.outputs])   # [(None, 1), (None, 4)]
# model.fit({"text": x_text, "meta": x_meta}, {"priority": y_p, "dept": y_d})
takeaways: Call layers on `keras.Input` placeholders, then `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)`
Supports several inputs and outputs, skip connections and shared layers
Name inputs and outputs and pass dicts to compile and fit
pitfalls: Creating a new layer object for each branch when you meant to share weights.

quiz.q: How do you make two inputs share the same Dense weights in the functional API?
options: Create two Dense layers with the same name
Call one Dense layer object on both inputs
quiz.explain: A layer object owns its weights, so calling it twice reuses them.

concepts.name: Losses, optimizers and metrics
concepts.summary: Match the loss to how your labels are written, choose an optimizer and learning rate, and see how metrics add up results across batches.
concepts.why: Mismatched loss and label formats, and poorly chosen learning rates, are the most common reasons a Keras model does not learn.
concepts.body:
**Losses** compare the right answers (`y_true`) with the predictions (`y_pred`) and return one number. Which one to use depends on the task and how the labels are written:

- `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy`: classification with integer labels like `2`. `CategoricalCrossentropy`: the same with **one-hot** labels, where class 2 of 4 is written `[0, 0, 1, 0]`.
- `BinaryCrossentropy`: yes/no targets in {0, 1}, including several independent yes/no questions per example.
- `MeanSquaredError`, `MeanAbsoluteError`, `Huber`: regression.

All classification losses take `from_logits=True` when predictions are raw scores. Any function `fn(y_true, y_pred)` that returns one loss per example also works.

**Optimizers** live in `keras.optimizers`: `Adam`, `AdamW`, `SGD(momentum=0.9)`, `RMSprop`, `Lion` and more; Adam is the usual starting point. Their most important setting is the **learning rate**: how big a step each update takes. Too big and training jumps around; too small and it crawls.

The learning rate can be a fixed number or a **learning-rate schedule** from `keras.optimizers.schedules` that changes it as training goes on, such as `CosineDecay` (shrinks it smoothly, optionally after a short warm-up) or `ExponentialDecay`. `AdamW`'s **weight decay** shrinks every weight slightly at each step, which makes memorising harder; `clipnorm` caps how big the gradients may get.

**Metrics** keep a running total: `update_state(y_true, y_pred)` adds a batch, `result()` gives the value so far and `reset_state()` clears it. That is why the accuracy `fit()` prints is over the whole epoch, not just the last batch. Accuracy metrics come in sparse and categorical versions matching the loss; `AUC`, `Precision` and `Recall` are also built in.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras

y_true = np.array([0, 2])
logits = np.array([[2.0, 0.5, -1.0], [0.1, 0.2, 3.0]], dtype="float32")

loss = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)
print(round(float(loss(y_true, logits)), 4))                 # 0.1755
probs = keras.ops.softmax(logits)
print(round(float(keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()(y_true, probs)), 4))  # 0.1755

acc = keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()
acc.update_state(y_true, logits)                 # 2 of 2 correct
acc.update_state(np.array([1]), np.array([[0.9, 0.1, 0.0]]))   # 0 of 1 correct
print(round(float(acc.result()), 3))             # 0.667  (accumulated)
acc.reset_state()

schedule = keras.optimizers.schedules.CosineDecay(1e-3, decay_steps=10_000)
opt = keras.optimizers.AdamW(learning_rate=schedule, weight_decay=1e-4)
takeaways: Sparse losses for integer labels, categorical for one-hot
The learning rate sets the step size; it can follow a schedule
Metrics accumulate with update_state / result / reset_state
pitfalls: Using CategoricalCrossentropy with integer labels, which fails with a shape error (or trains on the wrong targets).

quiz.q: Why is the accuracy printed by fit() at the end of an epoch an average over the epoch?
options: fit() recomputes it on the whole dataset
It is the last batch only
It is computed on validation data
Metrics are stateful and accumulate across batches until reset
quiz.explain: Metrics add up results with update_state and are reset at the start of each epoch.

concepts.name: Feeding data to fit()
concepts.summary: Train from NumPy arrays, TensorFlow's tf.data, PyTorch's DataLoader or a keras.utils.PyDataset, with any backend.
concepts.why: Real datasets often don't fit in memory; Keras 3 accepts plain arrays and the data-loading tools of TensorFlow and PyTorch.
concepts.body:
`fit()`, `evaluate()` and `predict()` accept several kinds of input, regardless of backend:

- **NumPy arrays** (or backend tensors): simplest; pass `batch_size` and let Keras shuffle each epoch.
- A **`tf.data.Dataset`** (TensorFlow's data-loading pipeline): yields batches already; do not pass `batch_size`. Works with JAX and PyTorch backends too, since Keras converts each batch.
- A **PyTorch `DataLoader`** (PyTorch's batch loader): yields batches; again no `batch_size`.
- A **`keras.utils.PyDataset`**: a Python class with `__len__` (number of batches) and `__getitem__(idx)` returning one batch. Pass `workers=` and `use_multiprocessing=` when creating it to load several batches at once.

For generators or infinite datasets, set `steps_per_epoch` so Keras knows when an epoch ends.

Batches can be `(x, y)` or `(x, y, sample_weight)`, and `x`/`y` can be dicts matching named inputs and outputs. `class_weight={0: 1.0, 1: 5.0}` makes mistakes on a rare class count five times as much in the loss.

Pick by need: NumPy for small data, tf.data for fast, heavy loading (especially with the TF or JAX backend), DataLoader if you already have PyTorch datasets, and PyDataset for custom Python loading code without extra dependencies.
concepts.code:
import math
import numpy as np
import keras

class RandomBatches(keras.utils.PyDataset):
    def __init__(self, n, batch_size, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)           # e.g. workers=4, use_multiprocessing=True
        self.n, self.batch_size = n, batch_size

    def __len__(self):                       # batches per epoch
        return math.ceil(self.n / self.batch_size)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):              # one batch
        size = min(self.batch_size, self.n - idx * self.batch_size)
        x = np.random.rand(size, 4).astype("float32")
        return x, x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((4,)), keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")
model.fit(RandomBatches(1000, 64), epochs=2, verbose=0)
# Also valid for fit(): NumPy arrays + batch_size, a tf.data.Dataset,
# or a torch DataLoader, with any backend.
takeaways: NumPy + batch_size, tf.data, torch DataLoader or PyDataset
Batched sources must not get a `batch_size` argument
`class_weight` and `sample_weight` reweight examples
pitfalls: Passing `batch_size` together with a dataset that is already batched.

quiz.q: What must PyDataset.__len__ return?
options: The number of batches per epoch
quiz.explain: Keras indexes batches 0..len-1, so __len__ counts batches.

concepts.name: Callbacks
concepts.summary: Hook into fit() with EarlyStopping, ModelCheckpoint, ReduceLROnPlateau, TensorBoard and your own Callback subclasses.
concepts.why: Callbacks add early stopping, saving, learning-rate changes and progress logs to training without writing your own loop.
concepts.body:
A **callback** is an object whose methods `fit()` calls at points in training: `on_train_begin`, `on_epoch_begin`/`on_epoch_end`, `on_train_batch_end` and so on. Pass a list with `fit(..., callbacks=[...])`.

The built-in ones cover most needs:

- `EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)`: **early stopping** ends training once the watched value (`monitor`) hasn't improved for `patience` epochs, and puts back the weights from the best epoch.
- `ModelCheckpoint("best.keras", save_best_only=True)`: save the model (or weights with a `.weights.h5` path) during training.
- `ReduceLROnPlateau(factor=0.5, patience=2)`: halve the learning rate (the size of each training step) when progress stalls.
- `LearningRateScheduler(fn)`: set the rate per epoch from a function.
- `TensorBoard(log_dir)`, `CSVLogger(path)`: write the loss and metrics of every epoch to files for charts.
- `BackupAndRestore(dir)`: resume automatically after an interruption.

To write your own, subclass `keras.callbacks.Callback`. Inside, `self.model` is the model being trained and `logs` is a dict of the current metrics (`loss`, `val_loss`...). Setting `self.model.stop_training = True` stops training.

Monitored names must match the logs exactly, including the `val_` prefix, which requires validation data.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras

x = np.random.rand(500, 4).astype("float32")
y = x.sum(axis=1)
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((4,)),
                          keras.layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
                          keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")

class PrintEvery(keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        if epoch % 20 == 0:
            print(f"epoch {epoch}: val_loss={logs['val_loss']:.4f}")

callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=5, restore_best_weights=True),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint("best.keras", monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True),
    keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=2),
    PrintEvery(),
]
history = model.fit(x, y, epochs=300, validation_split=0.2, callbacks=callbacks, verbose=0)
print("trained for", len(history.history["loss"]), "epochs")   # fewer than 300
takeaways: EarlyStopping + ModelCheckpoint + ReduceLROnPlateau is a solid default
Custom callbacks override `on_*` methods and read `logs`
Monitored keys must exist in logs (e.g. `val_loss` needs validation data)
pitfalls: Monitoring `val_accuracy` without passing validation data, so the callback never triggers (Keras only warns).

quiz.q: What does restore_best_weights=True add to EarlyStopping?
options: It saves the best model to disk
It restarts training from the best epoch
When stopping, it resets the model to the weights from the best epoch
It keeps training until val_loss stops decreasing
quiz.explain: Without it, the model keeps the weights of the last (worse) epoch.

concepts.name: Regularization and augmentation
concepts.summary: Fight overfitting with Dropout, weight penalties, BatchNormalization and augmentation layers that only act during training.
concepts.why: Most models start memorising before they stop improving; these tools close the gap between scores on training data and on validation data.
concepts.body:
**Overfitting** means the model memorises its training examples instead of learning the general pattern. It shows up as training loss falling while the loss on the validation set rises. Techniques against it are called **regularization**; Keras offers several, often combined:

- **Dropout(rate)**: during training, randomly sets a fraction of the previous layer's outputs to zero, so the model can't rely on any single one. Typical rates are 0.1 to 0.5.
- **Weight penalties**: `kernel_regularizer=keras.regularizers.L2(1e-4)` on a layer adds a penalty to the loss that grows with the size of the weights, nudging them to stay small. With Adam, prefer `AdamW(weight_decay=...)`, which shrinks the weights directly instead of through the gradient.
- **BatchNormalization**: rescales a layer's outputs to a steady average and spread, using each batch's own statistics while training and saved running averages when predicting. It mainly makes training stable but also helps a little against overfitting.
- **Data augmentation layers**: `RandomFlip`, `RandomRotation`, `RandomZoom`, `RandomContrast`, `RandomCrop` create randomly altered copies of each image every epoch (**data augmentation**).
- **Early stopping** with the callback.

All of these behave differently in training and when making predictions. Keras passes a `training` argument: `fit()` sets it to `True`, while `predict()`, `evaluate()` and plain `model(x)` use prediction behaviour. Augmentation layers are therefore no-ops at prediction time.

Regularization penalties appear in `model.losses` and are added to the main loss by `fit()`. Placing augmentation inside the model means exported models handle raw images; placing it in a `tf.data` pipeline runs it on the CPU, in parallel with training.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers, regularizers

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((32, 32, 3)),
    layers.RandomFlip("horizontal"),       # augmentation: training only
    layers.RandomRotation(0.1),
    layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False),
    layers.BatchNormalization(),
    layers.Activation("relu"),
    layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
    layers.Dropout(0.3),
    layers.Dense(10, kernel_regularizer=regularizers.L2(1e-4)),
])

x = np.random.rand(4, 32, 32, 3).astype("float32")
a = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(model(x, training=False))
b = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(model(x, training=False))
print(np.allclose(a, b))       # True: inference is deterministic
print(len(model.losses))       # 1  (the L2 penalty, added to the loss by fit)
takeaways: Dropout, weight decay, BatchNorm and augmentation combat overfitting
`training=True` in fit; prediction behaviour in predict and model(x)
Prefer AdamW's weight_decay over L2 penalties with Adam
pitfalls: Calling `model(x, training=True)` to make predictions, which applies dropout and random augmentation.

quiz.q: When you call model.predict(x), what do RandomFlip and Dropout layers do?
options: Apply random flips and dropout as in training
Act as identity: no flipping, no dropout
Flip but do not drop out
quiz.explain: Both only act when training=True; predict runs in prediction mode.

concepts.name: Preprocessing layers
concepts.summary: Normalize numeric features, encode categories and text with Normalization, StringLookup, IntegerLookup and TextVectorization, learning their state with adapt().
concepts.why: Putting preprocessing in layers keeps training and serving consistent and lets the model accept raw inputs.
concepts.body:
**Preprocessing** layers turn raw features into model-ready tensors. Many have state learned from data with **`adapt(data)`** before training:

- `Normalization(axis=-1)`: learns each feature's mean and variance (how spread out its values are), then outputs `(x - mean) / std`, so every feature sits around 0 with a spread of about 1.
- `Discretization(bin_boundaries=...)` or `num_bins=`: buckets numeric values.
- `StringLookup` and `IntegerLookup`: map categories to indices, with an **out-of-vocabulary** slot for values never seen during `adapt` (index 0 for one-hot output, 1 for integer output when index 0 is reserved for padding). `output_mode="one_hot"` or `"multi_hot"` gives encodings directly.
- `TextVectorization`: lowercases text, splits it into words and maps each word to an id.
- `Hashing`: maps categories to a fixed number of buckets, for huge or open-ended sets.
- Image layers: `Resizing`, `Rescaling(1/255)`, `CenterCrop`.

You can place them **inside the model**, so the saved model accepts plain text and numbers and serving cannot drift from training, or **in the input pipeline** (`dataset.map(layer)`), where they run on the CPU in the background while the model trains.

Some of these layers (the lookup and text layers) are implemented with TensorFlow ops; with the JAX or PyTorch backend they work in plain Python and inside `tf.data` pipelines, but not inside a compiled non-TF model, so put them in the data pipeline there.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers

data = np.array([[1.0, 200.0], [2.0, 300.0], [3.0, 400.0]], dtype="float32")
norm = layers.Normalization(axis=-1)
norm.adapt(data)                       # learns mean and variance per column
print(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(norm(data)).round(2))
# [[-1.22 -1.22]
#  [ 0.    0.  ]
#  [ 1.22  1.22]]

lookup = layers.StringLookup(vocabulary=["red", "green", "blue"], output_mode="one_hot")
print(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(lookup(np.array(["green", "purple"]))))
# [[0. 0. 1. 0.]
#  [1. 0. 0. 0.]]   column 0 = out-of-vocabulary
takeaways: `adapt()` learns state such as mean/variance or the list of known values
Inside the model: consistent serving; in tf.data: background CPU work
Lookup layers reserve an out-of-vocabulary index
pitfalls: Adapting a Normalization layer on all the data including the test examples, so their statistics leak into training.

quiz.q: What does Normalization.adapt(train_x) do?
options: Trains the whole model on train_x
Computes and stores per-feature mean and variance from train_x
quiz.explain: adapt sets the layer's non-trainable statistics; the layer then normalises any input with them.

concepts.name: Saving and exporting models
concepts.summary: Save full models in the .keras format, save or load weights only, and export a prediction-only version for serving.
concepts.why: You need to resume training, share models and ship them to apps or servers; each needs a different save format.
concepts.body:
Keras 3 has three ways to save a model:

- **`model.save("model.keras")`**: the native format, a zip with the architecture config, weights and optimizer state. Reload with `keras.saving.load_model("model.keras")`; the result is ready to `predict` or continue `fit`. Custom layers must be registered or passed via `custom_objects`.
- **`model.save_weights("model.weights.h5")`** and `load_weights(...)`: weights only. The file name must end in `.weights.h5`, and you rebuild the same architecture in code before loading.
- **`model.export("dir")`**: a version for making predictions only. By default it writes a TensorFlow SavedModel (needs TensorFlow installed) for TensorFlow's server and phone tools; recent versions also offer `format="onnx"`, a format many other tools can run.

The legacy `.h5` full-model format and the old `SavedModel` mode of `model.save()` from Keras 2 are no longer the way to save in Keras 3.

The `.keras` format is backend-independent: a model trained with JAX can be loaded under PyTorch. For checkpoints during training, use the `ModelCheckpoint` callback, which writes the same formats.

Loading runs in `safe_mode` by default, which refuses to load arbitrary Python code such as `Lambda` layers from untrusted files.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((3,)), keras.layers.Dense(2)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")

model.save("model.keras")                         # config + weights + optimizer
restored = keras.saving.load_model("model.keras")
x = np.ones((1, 3), dtype="float32")
print(np.allclose(model.predict(x, verbose=0),
                  restored.predict(x, verbose=0)))   # True

model.save_weights("model.weights.h5")            # weights only
clone = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((3,)), keras.layers.Dense(2)])
clone.load_weights("model.weights.h5")            # same architecture required
print(clone.get_weights()[0].shape)               # (3, 2)

# For serving (requires TensorFlow): model.export("export_dir")
takeaways: `.keras` = full model, backend-independent
`.weights.h5` = weights only, rebuild the architecture first
`model.export()` produces a prediction-only version for serving
pitfalls: Saving weights to a file not ending in `.weights.h5`, which Keras 3 rejects.

quiz.q: You trained with the JAX backend and saved model.keras. Can you load it with the PyTorch backend?
quiz.explain: The format stores the configuration and the weight values, not anything specific to one backend.

concepts.name: Subclassing keras.Model
concepts.summary: Write models as Python classes: create layers in __init__ and define the forward pass in call(), with a training flag.
concepts.why: Subclassing gives full Python flexibility for research architectures that are awkward as static graphs.
concepts.body:
For architectures with custom control flow, subclass **`keras.Model`**:

- Create layers in `__init__` and assign them to attributes; Keras tracks their weights automatically, including layers stored in lists or dicts.
- Implement `call(self, inputs, training=False)` with the **forward pass** (how inputs become outputs), passing `training` on to layers that need it (Dropout, BatchNorm).
- Call `super().__init__(**kwargs)` first so arguments like `name` work.

A subclassed model is used like any other: `compile`, `fit`, `evaluate`, `predict`. Weights are created on the first call, so call the model on a sample batch (or call `build`) before `summary()`.

Trade-offs compared with the functional API:

- More flexible: loops, conditionals and arbitrary Python inside `call`.
- Less visible: Keras cannot draw the network of layers or check shapes before running.
- Saving to `.keras` works, but to reload you must implement `get_config` (if `__init__` takes arguments) and register the class.

A good pattern is to build reusable blocks by subclassing `keras.layers.Layer` and assemble them with the functional API, getting flexibility where you need it and visibility everywhere else. With the PyTorch backend, a Keras model is also a `torch.nn.Module`.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import layers

class ResidualMLP(keras.Model):
    def __init__(self, units=64, n_classes=10, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.inp = layers.Dense(units, activation="relu")
        self.block = layers.Dense(units, activation="relu")
        self.drop = layers.Dropout(0.2)
        self.head = layers.Dense(n_classes)

    def call(self, x, training=False):
        h = self.inp(x)
        h = h + self.drop(self.block(h), training=training)   # residual connection
        return self.head(h)

model = ResidualMLP()
print(tuple(model(np.zeros((2, 20), dtype="float32")).shape))   # (2, 10)  builds weights
print(len(model.trainable_weights))                              # 6
model.compile(optimizer="adam",
              loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))
takeaways: Layers in `__init__`, computation in `call(inputs, training=False)`
Weights exist after the first call
More flexible but less visible than functional models
pitfalls: Ignoring the `training` argument, so dropout stays active or inactive in the wrong phase.

quiz.q: Why might model.summary() fail right after constructing a subclassed model?
options: Subclassed models do not support summary
The weights have not been created yet because the model has not been called or built
quiz.explain: Subclassed models build their layers on first call, when input shapes become known.

concepts.name: keras.ops: backend-agnostic math
concepts.summary: Write maths once with keras.ops (NumPy-like functions plus neural-network operations) and keras.random, and run it on any backend.
concepts.why: Custom layers, losses and metrics stay portable across JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch only if they use keras.ops.
concepts.body:
**`keras.ops`** is Keras 3's set of tensor functions that work on every backend. It implements most of the NumPy API (`ops.sum`, `ops.matmul`, `ops.reshape`, `ops.where`, `ops.einsum`...) plus neural-network functions (`ops.softmax`, `ops.relu`, `ops.conv`, `ops.one_hot`, `ops.logsumexp`) and core control flow (`ops.cond`, `ops.while_loop`, `ops.scan`). Each call dispatches to the active backend, so code written with it runs on JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch alike.

Practical rules:

- Inside custom layers, losses and metrics, use `keras.ops` instead of `tf.*`, `jnp.*` or `torch.*`, unless you deliberately target one backend.
- `ops.convert_to_tensor(x)` makes a backend tensor; `ops.convert_to_numpy(t)` brings it back.
- Dtypes are strings: `"float32"`, `"int32"`, `"bfloat16"`.

Randomness goes through **`keras.random`**: `normal`, `uniform`, `dropout`, `shuffle`. Pass a seed or, better, a `keras.random.SeedGenerator`, which keeps its position in the random sequence in a variable, so random ops give fresh numbers on every call even inside compiled code and JAX's stateless functions (functions that may not keep hidden state).

Because results are backend-native, printing them shows backend types; convert to NumPy for portable output.
concepts.code:
import keras
from keras import ops

x = ops.arange(6, dtype="float32")
m = ops.reshape(x, (2, 3))
print(ops.convert_to_numpy(ops.sum(m, axis=0)))                   # [3. 5. 7.]
print(ops.convert_to_numpy(ops.matmul(m, ops.transpose(m))))      # [[ 5. 14.] [14. 50.]]
print(ops.convert_to_numpy(ops.softmax(ops.array([0.0, 0.0]))))   # [0.5 0.5]
print(ops.convert_to_numpy(ops.where(m > 2, m, 0.0)))             # [[0. 0. 0.] [3. 4. 5.]]
print(ops.convert_to_numpy(ops.one_hot(ops.array([2, 0]), 3)))    # [[0. 0. 1.] [1. 0. 0.]]

seed = keras.random.SeedGenerator(42)
noise = keras.random.normal((2, 3), seed=seed)   # reproducible on every backend
print(tuple(noise.shape))                        # (2, 3)
takeaways: `keras.ops` = NumPy API + NN ops, on every backend
Use it in custom layers, losses and metrics for portability
Use `keras.random` with a SeedGenerator for randomness
pitfalls: Calling `tf.*` functions in a custom layer, which breaks as soon as the backend is JAX or PyTorch.

quiz.q: Why use keras.random.SeedGenerator instead of an integer seed inside a layer?
options: It keeps RNG state as a variable, so each call draws new numbers even in compiled or stateless code
It makes results identical on all backends
quiz.explain: A fixed integer seed would repeat the same numbers on every call inside a compiled function.

concepts.name: Writing custom layers
concepts.summary: Subclass keras.layers.Layer with build() and add_weight(), implement call() with keras.ops, and make it serializable with get_config().
concepts.why: Custom layers are how you package new ideas so they work with fit, saving and every backend.
concepts.body:
A custom layer subclasses **`keras.layers.Layer`** and usually implements:

- `__init__(self, ..., **kwargs)`: store the layer's settings (such as the number of units); call `super().__init__(**kwargs)`.
- `build(self, input_shape)`: create weights with `self.add_weight(shape, initializer, trainable=True, name=...)`. Creating weights here, rather than in `__init__`, lets the layer adapt to the input size it first sees.
- `call(self, inputs, training=None)`: the computation, written with `keras.ops` for portability.
- `get_config(self)`: return the `__init__` arguments merged with `super().get_config()`, so the layer can be re-created with `from_config` when a saved model is loaded.

Decorate the class with `@keras.saving.register_keras_serializable(package="...")` so `load_model` can find it without `custom_objects`.

Other useful hooks: `self.add_loss(value)` to add an extra penalty to the loss, non-trainable weights (`trainable=False`) for state like moving averages (update them with `assign`), and `compute_output_shape` if Keras cannot infer it.

Nested layers assigned as attributes are tracked automatically, so their weights appear in `layer.weights`. Test a new layer by calling it on a NumPy batch, checking output shapes, and round-tripping it through `get_config`/`from_config`.
takeaways: Create weights in `build` with `add_weight`
Write `call` with `keras.ops` for portability
Implement `get_config` and register the class for saving
pitfalls: Creating weights in `call`, which makes new weights on every call.

quiz.q: Why create weights in build() rather than __init__?
options: build receives the input shape, so the layer can size its weights to the data it first sees
quiz.explain: Deferring creation to build lets layers like Dense infer their input dimension.

concepts.name: Custom losses and metrics
concepts.summary: Write losses as functions or Loss subclasses, and metrics that keep running totals as Metric subclasses with add_variable, update_state and result.
concepts.why: Business objectives and research ideas rarely match the built-in losses and metrics exactly.
concepts.body:
**Custom losses**: any function `loss(y_true, y_pred)` built from `keras.ops` that returns one value per sample works. Keras applies sample weights and averages them into a single number for you. If the loss has settings that must be saved, subclass `keras.losses.Loss`, implement `call(y_true, y_pred)` and `get_config`.

**Custom metrics** must accumulate across batches, so they are classes:

- Subclass `keras.metrics.Metric`.
- In `__init__`, create state with `self.add_variable(shape=(), initializer="zeros", name=...)`.
- `update_state(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None)`: update the variables with `assign_add`.
- `result()`: compute the metric from the state.
- `reset_state()`: the default resets every variable to its initializer, which is usually enough.

Why not compute a metric as a mean of per-batch values? Because many metrics are not averages of per-batch results: precision (the share of 'yes' predictions that were right), AUC, or any percentage of a total. Keeping sums and counts gives the exact epoch-level value.

For quantities that are not functions of `(y_true, y_pred)`, such as a penalty computed inside a layer, use `self.add_loss(...)` in the layer, or override `compute_loss` in the model.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import keras
from keras import ops
def huber_like(y_true, y_pred, delta=1.0):         # a plain function is a valid loss
    err = ops.abs(y_true - y_pred)
    sq = 0.5 * err ** 2
    return ops.mean(ops.where(err < delta, sq, delta * (err - 0.5 * delta)), axis=-1)

class MeanAbsPct(keras.metrics.Metric):
    def __init__(self, name="mape", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(name=name, **kwargs)
        self.total = self.add_variable(shape=(), initializer="zeros", name="total")
        self.count = self.add_variable(shape=(), initializer="zeros", name="count")
    def update_state(self, y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None):
        pct = ops.abs((y_true - y_pred) / y_true) * 100.0
        self.total.assign_add(ops.sum(pct))
        self.count.assign_add(ops.sum(ops.ones_like(pct)))
    def result(self):
        return self.total / self.count

m = MeanAbsPct()
m.update_state(np.array([100.0, 200.0], "float32"), np.array([110.0, 190.0], "float32"))
print(float(m.result()))                           # 7.5  (10% and 5% errors)
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((3,)), keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=huber_like, metrics=[MeanAbsPct()])
takeaways: A loss can be any `fn(y_true, y_pred)` built from keras.ops
Metrics keep sums/counts in variables: update_state, result, reset_state
Use `add_loss` for terms that do not depend on targets
pitfalls: Averaging per-batch metric values for metrics that are not batch-decomposable, like precision.

quiz.q: Why does a custom Metric keep total and count variables instead of averaging per-batch results?
options: So the epoch value is exact even when batches differ in size or the metric is not a simple average
quiz.explain: Accumulating raw sums gives the true dataset-level value regardless of batch sizes.

concepts.name: Customizing what fit() does
concepts.summary: Override train_step in a keras.Model subclass to control each training step while keeping fit(), callbacks and metrics.
concepts.why: Models trained against each other (GANs), contrastive learning and many research setups need custom steps, and this keeps all of fit()'s conveniences.
concepts.body:
`fit()` calls `model.train_step(data)` for every batch. Overriding it gives you control over the step while keeping callbacks, progress bars, distribution and `evaluate`/`predict`. Because gradients are computed differently on each backend, the step is written in that backend's style:

- **TensorFlow**: compute the loss inside a `tf.GradientTape`, get gradients with `tape.gradient`, and apply with `self.optimizer.apply(grads, self.trainable_variables)`.
- **PyTorch**: call `self.zero_grad()`, compute the loss, `loss.backward()`, collect `v.value.grad` for each trainable variable, and apply under `torch.no_grad()`.
- **JAX**: steps are **stateless**, keeping no hidden changing values: `train_step(self, state, data)` receives the current variable values and returns new ones, and uses `self.stateless_call` and `self.optimizer.stateless_apply`.

In every version, use `self.compute_loss(x=x, y=y, y_pred=y_pred)` to get the loss configured in `compile` (including any extra penalties layers added), and update `self.metrics`. Return a dict of metric results; those become the logs callbacks see.

Override `test_step` the same way for custom evaluation. If you need several optimizers (as in a **GAN**, where one network makes fake examples and another learns to spot them), override `compile` to accept them. For full control without fit(), write a training loop from scratch with the same building blocks.
concepts.code:
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "tensorflow"
import numpy as np
import keras
import tensorflow as tf

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        x, y = data
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            y_pred = self(x, training=True)
            loss = self.compute_loss(x=x, y=y, y_pred=y_pred)
        grads = tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_variables)
        self.optimizer.apply(grads, self.trainable_variables)
        for metric in self.metrics:
            if metric.name == "loss":
                metric.update_state(loss)
            else:
                metric.update_state(y, y_pred)
        return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}

inputs = keras.Input((32,))
model = CustomModel(inputs, keras.layers.Dense(1)(inputs))
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])
model.fit(np.random.rand(256, 32), np.random.rand(256, 1), epochs=2, verbose=0)
takeaways: Override `train_step` to customise the step but keep fit()
Gradient code is backend-specific; JAX steps are stateless
Use `self.compute_loss` and update `self.metrics`; return their results
pitfalls: Forgetting to update metrics in the custom step, so fit() logs stale or zero values.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of overriding train_step instead of writing a full training loop?
options: It runs faster on every backend
You keep fit()'s callbacks, progress bars, distribution and evaluate/predict
quiz.explain: train_step plugs custom logic into fit() so all its features keep working.

concepts.name: Transfer learning and fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Reuse pretrained models from keras.applications or KerasHub: freeze them, train a new head, then fine-tune with a low learning rate.
concepts.why: Starting from a model someone already trained on lots of data gives strong results with little data and computing power.
concepts.body:
**Transfer learning** starts from a **pretrained** model, one already trained by someone else on a large dataset, and reuses what it learned for your task. In Keras:

- `keras.applications` provides image models trained on **ImageNet**, a public set of over a million labelled photos (ResNet, EfficientNetV2, ConvNeXt, MobileNetV3...). `include_top=False` drops their final classification layers so you can add your own.
- **KerasHub** (`keras_hub`) provides pretrained presets for text, vision and audio, including large language models, all built on Keras 3.

The standard two-phase recipe:

1. **Feature extraction**: set `base.trainable = False` to freeze the pretrained weights, put a new **head** (a few fresh layers ending in your classes) on top, and train only the head. Call the base with `training=False` so its BatchNormalization layers keep their saved averages even later, when you unfreeze them.
2. **Fine-tuning**, training the whole thing a little more: set `base.trainable = True` (or unfreeze only the top blocks), **recompile** so the change takes effect, and train a few epochs with a learning rate 10-100x smaller.

Preprocessing must match what the model was trained with. Each application has a `preprocess_input` function; some, like EfficientNetV2 and ConvNeXt, include preprocessing in the model and expect raw 0-255 pixels.

Setting `trainable` on a model or layer also applies to every layer inside it, and frozen weights appear in `non_trainable_weights`.
concepts.code:
import keras
from keras import layers

base = keras.applications.EfficientNetV2B0(
    include_top=False, weights="imagenet", input_shape=(224, 224, 3))
base.trainable = False                        # 1) freeze pretrained weights

inputs = keras.Input((224, 224, 3))           # raw 0-255 pixels for EfficientNetV2
x = base(inputs, training=False)              # keep BatchNorm in inference mode
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.2)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(5)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

loss = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss=loss, metrics=["accuracy"])
# model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=5)    # trains the head only

base.trainable = True                         # 2) fine-tune everything
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-5), loss=loss, metrics=["accuracy"])
# model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=3)    # recompiled, tiny LR
print(len(model.trainable_weights) > 2)       # True
takeaways: Freeze, train a new head, then unfreeze and fine-tune with a tiny learning rate
Call the base with `training=False` to protect BatchNorm statistics
Recompile after changing `trainable`
pitfalls: Changing `trainable` without recompiling, so the change is not applied to training.

quiz.q: Why call the pretrained base with training=False even when fine-tuning?
options: To keep BatchNorm layers using their learned moving statistics instead of small-batch statistics
quiz.explain: training=False only affects layers like BatchNorm and Dropout; the weights can still be trainable.

concepts.name: Mixed precision
concepts.summary: Train faster with the mixed_bfloat16 or mixed_float16 dtype policy, keeping variables and outputs in float32.
concepts.why: Mixed precision can roughly double training speed on modern GPUs and TPUs on every Keras backend.
concepts.body:
A 16-bit float takes half the memory of a float32 and is much faster on modern GPUs and TPUs, but it is less precise. **Mixed precision** gets the speed with little of the risk: layers compute in 16 bits while the weights are stored in float32, so small updates aren't rounded away. Keras sets this with a **dtype policy**:

```python
keras.config.set_dtype_policy("mixed_bfloat16")
```

Every layer created afterwards gets `compute_dtype` bfloat16 and `variable_dtype` float32. Use `"mixed_bfloat16"` on TPUs and recent GPUs (NVIDIA Ampere and newer); use `"mixed_float16"` on older GPUs that have **tensor cores** (fast 16-bit matrix units). **bfloat16** keeps float32's range of sizes, while **float16** has a much smaller range.

Guidelines:

- Keep the model's **output in float32** by giving the last layer `dtype="float32"` (often a final `Activation("softmax", dtype="float32")`).
- With `mixed_float16`, very small gradients **underflow** (round to zero), so **loss scaling** is needed: multiply the loss by a large number before computing gradients, and divide the gradients back afterwards. A `LossScaleOptimizer` does this; `compile()` wraps your optimizer automatically. In a custom train step, call `optimizer.scale_loss(loss)` before computing gradients.
- bfloat16 has float32's range and does not need loss scaling.
- Individual layers can override the policy with `dtype=...`.

Set the policy before building the model, and reset it with `keras.config.set_dtype_policy("float32")` if later code should run in full precision. Measure: on CPUs and older GPUs mixed precision can be slower.
concepts.code:
import keras
from keras import layers

keras.config.set_dtype_policy("mixed_bfloat16")    # or "mixed_float16" on older GPUs

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((512,)),
    layers.Dense(1024, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(10),
    layers.Activation("softmax", dtype="float32"),  # numerically sensitive output
])
d = model.layers[0]
print(d.dtype_policy.name, d.compute_dtype, d.variable_dtype)
# mixed_bfloat16 bfloat16 float32
print(model.layers[-1].compute_dtype)              # float32

model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy")
# with "mixed_float16", compile() wraps the optimizer in a LossScaleOptimizer

keras.config.set_dtype_policy("float32")           # reset the global policy
takeaways: Mixed policies: 16-bit compute, float32 variables
Keep the final output layer in float32
float16 needs loss scaling (automatic in compile); bfloat16 does not
pitfalls: Setting the policy after the model was built, so existing layers keep float32.

quiz.q: Under the mixed_bfloat16 policy, what are a Dense layer's compute and variable dtypes?
quiz.explain: Mixed policies compute in the 16-bit type but store variables in float32.

concepts.name: Stateless training with JAX
concepts.summary: How Keras runs on JAX: stateless_call and stateless_apply pass variable values explicitly, enabling jax.jit and jax.grad over Keras models.
concepts.why: It is how fit() works under JAX and what you need to combine Keras models with custom JAX code.
concepts.body:
JAX can only compile and differentiate **pure functions**: functions whose result depends only on their arguments and that change nothing outside themselves. Keras variables are mutable, so on the JAX backend Keras provides **stateless** versions of everything that touches state:

- `model.stateless_call(trainable_values, non_trainable_values, x, training=...)` runs the forward pass using the arrays you pass in and returns `(outputs, new_non_trainable_values)`, for example updated BatchNorm statistics.
- `optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_values, grads, trainable_values)` returns new trainable values and new optimizer values.
- Metrics have `stateless_update_state` and `stateless_result`.

A training step is then a pure function from `(state, batch)` to `(loss, new_state)`, which you can wrap in `jax.jit`, differentiate with `jax.value_and_grad(..., has_aux=True)`, or split across several devices with JAX's tools. The state is just lists of arrays gathered from `model.trainable_variables`, `model.non_trainable_variables` and `optimizer.variables`.

After the loop, write the final values back with `variable.assign(value)` so the Keras model (and `model.save`) reflect the training.

This is exactly what `fit()` does internally on JAX, and it is the pattern to use when combining Keras layers with Flax (a JAX neural-network library) or your own JAX code. Remember to `optimizer.build(model.trainable_variables)` before reading its variables.
concepts.code:
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"
import jax, keras, numpy as np
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((4,)), keras.layers.Dense(1)])
optimizer = keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.1)
optimizer.build(model.trainable_variables)
loss_fn = keras.losses.MeanSquaredError()
def compute_loss(tv, ntv, x, y):
    y_pred, ntv = model.stateless_call(tv, ntv, x, training=True)
    return loss_fn(y, y_pred), ntv
@jax.jit
def train_step(state, x, y):
    tv, ntv, ov = state
    (loss, ntv), grads = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss, has_aux=True)(tv, ntv, x, y)
    tv, ov = optimizer.stateless_apply(ov, grads, tv)
    return loss, (tv, ntv, ov)
state = ([v.value for v in model.trainable_variables],
         [v.value for v in model.non_trainable_variables],
         [v.value for v in optimizer.variables])
x = np.random.rand(256, 4).astype("float32"); y = x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
for _ in range(300):
    loss, state = train_step(state, x, y)
for var, val in zip(model.trainable_variables, state[0]):
    var.assign(val)                                  # write results back
print(float(loss) < 0.01)                            # True
takeaways: JAX needs pure functions; Keras offers stateless_call / stateless_apply
State = lists of trainable, non-trainable and optimizer values
Assign final values back to the Keras variables
pitfalls: Forgetting to write the trained values back, then saving a model with its initial weights.

quiz.q: What does model.stateless_call return besides the outputs?
options: Updated non-trainable variable values (e.g. BatchNorm statistics)
quiz.explain: Forward passes can change non-trainable state, which must be returned explicitly in a pure function.

concepts.name: The keras.distribution API
concepts.summary: Split data and model weights across devices with DeviceMesh, LayoutMap, DataParallel and ModelParallel (JAX backend).
concepts.why: Large models need their weights split across several GPUs or TPUs; Keras lets you describe the split without rewriting the model.
concepts.body:
**`keras.distribution`** describes how to place variables and data on many devices. It is currently implemented for the **JAX** backend (other backends use their own tools, like `tf.distribute` or PyTorch's DDP/FSDP).

The building blocks:

- `keras.distribution.list_devices()` lists accelerators.
- A **`DeviceMesh(shape, axis_names, devices)`** (a **device mesh**) arranges devices in a named grid, for example 2 x 4 with axes `("batch", "model")`.
- **`DataParallel()`**: **data parallelism**, a full copy of the model on every device and a different slice of each batch on each. One line for multi-GPU training.
- **`ModelParallel(layout_map=..., batch_dim_name="batch")`**: **model parallelism**, where each weight tensor is split into pieces held by different devices (**sharding**). A **`LayoutMap`** says how: it matches variable paths by pattern and gives each a layout. `(None, "model")` splits a kernel's second axis across the mesh's `model` axis and keeps a full copy of the first axis on every device.

Activate a distribution with `keras.distribution.set_distribution(...)` **before** creating the model, so variables are created already split; then `fit()` works as usual and the batch is split along the batch axis.

Sharded dimensions must be divisible by the mesh axis size. Under the hood Keras uses JAX's sharding, and JAX's compiler inserts the data exchanges between devices, so the model code itself stays unchanged.
concepts.code:
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"
import keras

devices = keras.distribution.list_devices()          # e.g. 8 GPUs or TPU cores
mesh = keras.distribution.DeviceMesh(
    shape=(2, len(devices) // 2), axis_names=("batch", "model"), devices=devices)

layout_map = keras.distribution.LayoutMap(mesh)
layout_map["dense_1/kernel"] = (None, "model")   # split output columns across "model"
layout_map["dense_1/bias"] = ("model",)

keras.distribution.set_distribution(
    keras.distribution.ModelParallel(layout_map=layout_map, batch_dim_name="batch"))

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((1024,)),
                          keras.layers.Dense(4096, name="dense_1"),
                          keras.layers.Dense(10, name="dense_2")])
# Variables are created sharded; fit() splits each batch along "batch".
# Pure data parallelism instead:
#   keras.distribution.set_distribution(keras.distribution.DataParallel())
takeaways: DeviceMesh names device axes; LayoutMap maps variable paths to layouts
DataParallel for replication, ModelParallel for sharded weights
Set the distribution before building the model (JAX backend)
pitfalls: Setting the distribution after the model exists, so its variables are not sharded.

quiz.q: With a mesh axis 'model' of size 4, which Dense kernel can use the layout (None, 'model')?
quiz.explain: The sharded dimension must be divisible by the axis size; 4096 is, 10 is not.

concepts.name: Serialization and layer internals
concepts.summary: What a .keras file contains, how get_config/from_config rebuild objects, safe_mode, and how Keras tracks variables in layers.
concepts.why: Fixing load failures, writing robust custom objects and loading untrusted models safely require knowing these internals.
concepts.body:
A **`.keras` file** is a zip archive with three parts: `config.json` (the serialised architecture and compile config), `model.weights.h5` (the variable values, keyed by layer structure) and `metadata.json` (Keras version, date). Loading reads the config, re-creates each object, builds it, and then loads weights in order.

Re-creation relies on **serialization**, turning each object into saveable data and back: each object's `get_config()` must return the arguments its `__init__` needs, and the class must be found by name. Built-in classes are found automatically; your own need `@keras.saving.register_keras_serializable` or `custom_objects=`. Most "unknown layer" or "unexpected keyword argument" load errors come from a missing registration or an incomplete `get_config`.

**`safe_mode=True`** (the default) refuses to load Python **bytecode** (a function's compiled form), such as the functions inside `Lambda` layers, because it could run arbitrary code. Only pass `safe_mode=False` for files you trust; better, replace `Lambda` layers with small registered custom layers.

**Tracking**: when you assign a layer, variable, list or dict of layers to an attribute, Keras records it, which is how `weights`, saving and `trainable` propagation find everything. Every weight is a `keras.Variable` wrapping a backend array, with a `path` naming where it lives. Layers are built lazily in `build()`, and the functional API records an operation graph of `KerasTensor`s that is replayed when you call the model.
concepts.code:
import zipfile
import keras

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((3,)), keras.layers.Dense(2, name="head")])
model.save("m.keras")
print(sorted(zipfile.ZipFile("m.keras").namelist()))
# ['config.json', 'metadata.json', 'model.weights.h5']

cfg = model.get_layer("head").get_config()
print(cfg["units"], cfg["activation"])            # 2 linear
rebuilt = keras.layers.Dense.from_config(cfg)     # a fresh, unbuilt Dense(2)

kernel = model.get_layer("head").kernel
print(isinstance(kernel, keras.Variable), kernel.path)   # True .../head/kernel

lam = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((3,)), keras.layers.Lambda(lambda t: t * 2)])
lam.save("lam.keras")
try:
    keras.saving.load_model("lam.keras")          # safe_mode=True by default
except ValueError:
    print("blocked: Lambda bytecode needs safe_mode=False")
takeaways: `.keras` = config.json + model.weights.h5 + metadata.json
`get_config` + registration let Keras rebuild custom objects
safe_mode blocks deserialising Python code such as Lambda layers
pitfalls: Loading untrusted .keras files with `safe_mode=False`.

quiz.q: Why does load_model refuse a model with a Lambda layer by default?
options: Deserialising the Lambda's Python bytecode could execute arbitrary code, so safe_mode blocks it
quiz.explain: safe_mode protects against code execution from untrusted files; trusted ones can opt out.
